mcqs.question: A checkout flow only ever processes payments through Stripe, with no other provider planned or requested. Does it need a PaymentStrategy extension point?
options: Yes — extension points should be added wherever behavior theoretically could vary
No — without a second concrete case today or a documented near-term one, the seam has no real variation to support
Yes — every payment-related code path should be pluggable by default for security reasons
No — extension points are only ever appropriate for UI code, never for payment logic
mcqs.explanation: The test is a second real or documented case, not theoretical possibility. Adding a seam wherever behavior theoretically could vary describes premature abstraction, not good design; there's no security rule requiring payment code to be pluggable; extension points aren't limited to UI code either.

mcqs.question: A team builds a NotificationStrategy interface with a single EmailNotificationStrategy implementation, expecting to add SMS later. What's the actual cost they're paying right now?
options: The interface makes email notifications literally impossible to send
Nothing — interfaces have no cost until a second implementation exists
The code will fail to compile until SMS support is added
Every reader has to trace through the abstraction to find the one class that actually runs, for no current benefit
mcqs.explanation: Premature abstraction costs readability and indirection immediately — every reader traces through the interface to reach the single real implementation. Email notifications still work fine through the interface; the cost isn't zero just because there's one implementation; and nothing here fails to compile.

mcqs.question: A team builds a generic plugin framework for a feature with exactly one real caller today, anticipating future needs. What commonly goes wrong when a second real use case eventually shows up?
options: The guessed extension points often don't match how the real second case actually varies, forcing rework anyway
The second use case always fits the guessed-at extension points perfectly
Frameworks built this way never need to be modified again
The original single caller stops working once a second one is added
mcqs.explanation: Guessing at future variation usually gets the shape wrong — the real second case often doesn't fit the imagined seams, so the team reworks the abstraction anyway, paying the framework's cost without the benefit. The other options describe outcomes that specifically don't happen in this pitfall.

mcqs.question: In the shipping example, what does moving from a hard-coded conditional to a feature-flagged rule lookup actually change?
options: It makes the shipping calculation run without any conditional logic at all
It removes the need for the ShippingRule interface entirely
Adding a new region's pricing means adding a rule instead of editing a growing if/else chain
It guarantees shipping costs are calculated correctly for every region automatically
mcqs.explanation: The refactor's benefit is isolating each rule so a new region is an addition, not an edit to shared conditional logic — the lookup itself is still a form of branching, just contained. It doesn't eliminate correctness bugs automatically, and the interface is what enables this benefit, not something removed by it.
